career-manager-view.title: How might my manager see me?
career-manager-view.summary: Explore how work habits may signal trust, readiness, or concern.
career-manager-view.focus: First use two distinct symbolic interpretations to explore how the supplied cards may suggest my manager sees my work habits and readiness. Do not state their judgment as fact; briefly add the most direct evidence from actual feedback, delegated authority, or assignments that could revise the reading and one low-pressure way to verify it.

career-workplace-image.title: How might coworkers see me?
career-workplace-image.summary: Separate collaborative strengths from traits others may misread.
career-workplace-image.focus: First use two distinct symbolic interpretations to explore the impression coworkers may form while working with me. Do not invent any coworker's private thoughts; briefly add evidence from repeated collaboration responses or direct comments that could revise the reading.

career-visible-contribution.title: Is my contribution visible?
career-visible-contribution.summary: Separate actual contribution from what the organization can readily see.
career-visible-contribution.focus: Use two symbolic interpretations to separate the contribution I actually make from how readily the organization may recognize it. Do not state a performance judgment as fact; identify evidence in feedback, decision participation, or work records that could verify the reading and one small action that makes the contribution clearer.

career-manager-expectations.title: What might my manager expect?
career-manager-expectations.summary: Separate stated responsibilities from expectations I may be assuming.
career-manager-expectations.focus: First use two distinct symbolic interpretations to explore what my manager may expect from my work. Do not state their thoughts as fact; briefly name evidence from stated goals, actual feedback, or assigned roles that could revise the reading and one question that could verify the expectation.

career-stay-or-prepare.title: Should I stay or get ready to move?
career-stay-or-prepare.summary: Compare what is worth trying here with the effort of moving.
career-stay-or-prepare.focus: Compare what may still be worth testing in the current role with the effort and tradeoffs involved in preparing for change. Do not treat either path as a settled outcome; name evidence to check first and one low-cost preparation step.

career-opportunity-cost.title: What would I give up for this opportunity?
career-opportunity-cost.summary: Compare what you gain with time, focus, or freedom you lose.
career-opportunity-cost.focus: Read both the choices this opportunity may open and the time, attention, or role flexibility it may reduce. Do not predict compensation or success; identify a condition to verify and one small exploratory action before committing.

career-interview-strengths.title: Which strengths should I show in an interview?
career-interview-strengths.summary: Choose role-relevant evidence instead of listing every strength.
career-interview-strengths.focus: Find the strengths I can connect to the target role and the real experience that supports them instead of listing every positive trait. Do not predict an offer; identify one piece of evidence and one small answer experiment that can show the strength clearly.

career-application-direction.title: Does my application direction fit me?
career-application-direction.summary: Compare attractive roles with conditions I can actually sustain.
career-application-direction.focus: Compare the roles attracting me with the strengths I use well and the work conditions I can actually sustain. Do not predict a hiring result; identify one piece of evidence in a posting, experience record, or exploratory conversation that can verify the direction.

career-underused-strength.title: Which strength am I overlooking?
career-underused-strength.summary: Find where a familiar skill already helps your work.
career-underused-strength.focus: Explore a strength I may overlook because it feels familiar and the work conditions in which it becomes useful. Do not define my personality as fact; connect the reading to a small record or experiment that could reveal evidence of that strength.

career-growth-experience.title: What experience do I need next?
career-growth-experience.summary: Find the next experience that builds on what you do well.
career-growth-experience.focus: Read what experience may be missing between my current strengths and the next stage I want to explore. Do not predict a promotion or selection result; suggest a small, reversible attempt that can reveal learning rather than guarantee an outcome.

career-role-fit.title: Does my current role fit my strengths?
career-role-fit.summary: Compare strengths I use well with what the role demands.
career-role-fit.focus: Separate the strengths I use naturally in my current role from demands I repeatedly stretch to cover. Do not frame role fit as a fixed personality trait; suggest one small experiment that can verify which work conditions fit and which do not.

career-collaboration-role.title: What role do I repeat when teamwork gets hard?
career-collaboration-role.summary: Look past who is right to the roles and assumptions that repeat.
career-collaboration-role.focus: Explore the role I may repeatedly take in collaboration and the expectations people may understand differently. Do not claim to know another person's intent; suggest one word or action that could clarify responsibilities.

career-sustainable-boundary.title: Which work limit should I set first?
career-sustainable-boundary.summary: Find one lasting limit for time, responsibility, or communication.
career-sustainable-boundary.focus: Read the pattern that may be consuming energy at work and the first boundary to clarify around time, responsibility, or communication. Do not assess my health; name one small boundary and a review point if it is not respected.

career-manager-mismatch.title: Why do my manager and I keep misaligning?
career-manager-mismatch.summary: Look for repeated differences in standards, reporting, and pace.
career-manager-mismatch.focus: Explore recurring differences in work standards, reporting, or pace when my manager and I misalign. Do not claim either person's intent; identify a role or expectation we may understand differently, one question that can verify it, and one small change to test in the next task.
